name: Aymara lordships of the Altiplano (Colla, Lupaca, Pacajes, Charka and neighbours)
summary: The group of rival Aymara-speaking kingdoms and lordships that rose around Lake Titicaca and across the Bolivian Altiplano after Tiwanaku fell, and that the Inca absorbed into Collasuyo while leaving them some autonomy.

knownFor.label: Chullpa burial towers
knownFor.note: Tower-shaped mausoleums for leaders, with a different design in each society.

location.value: The Qullaw, the Altiplano around Lake Titicaca between Cuzco and Potosí; Urcosuyu lay on the western side of the lake and Umasuyu on the eastern side.
location.source: Wikipedia: Aymara lordships (page read); Encyclopedia.com: Aymara

terrain.value: A high plateau, plus lower-altitude colonies in valleys, Pacific coastal valleys and the Amazon basin, described by John Murra as discontinuous 'vertical archipelagos'.

economicBase.value: Main settlements stood on valley sides or on the plateau, where people grazed llamas and alpacas, used salt deposits, and grew potatoes and quinoa.

tradeRoutes.value: The Aymara practice of founding colonies in the eastern valleys and on the coast was tolerated under Inca rule.

governmentType.value: A group of rival kingdoms and lordships, described as a confederation of diarchies: each society had two leaders. The twelve major ones were Canchis, Canas, Collas, Lupacas, Pacajes, Carangas, Soras, Charcas, Quillacas, Cara-caras, Chuis and Chichas.

stability.value: There was often fierce competition among the kingdoms, which is why they were well fortified.

armyAndTech.value: The kingdoms were well fortified militarily; one account says they lived inland in fortified settlements.
armyAndTech.source: Encyclopedia.com: Aymara; Wikipedia: Pre-Columbian Bolivia (mirror excerpts)

majorWars.value: Inca conquest. One account has Pachacuti defeating the Collas and capturing their ruler near Hatunqulla; another says Inca expansion southward began after about 1440; a third says several kingdoms rebelled against the Inca in 1470; and Wikipedia's Aymara article says the Altiplano fell under Huayna Capac (reigned 1493 to 1523), exact date unknown.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Aymara lordships (page read); Encyclopedia.com: Aymara; Wikipedia: Pre-Columbian Bolivia (mirror excerpts); Wikipedia: Aymara people (search excerpt)

territoryChange.value: Destroyed Colla towns were resettled with mitmakuna (forced settlers); the Inca called all Aymara kingdoms 'Collas' and the territory became part of Collasuyo.

alliancesRivals.value: Viracocha Inca is said to have played the Collas and Lupacas against each other; the Colla ruler attacked the Lupacas first and the Collas became dominant in the Qullaw before the Inca army arrived.

languageWriting.value: Aymara and Puquina are named, with Uru and Quechua also listed; there was no writing.

artsArchitecture.value: Most kingdoms buried leaders in tower-shaped mausoleums called chullpas, with a different design in each society.

socialStructure.value: Dual leadership (two leaders per society) ran through all of them.

sharedIdentity.value: The Aymara kept some autonomy under Inca rule and survive as a people of about two million across Bolivia, Peru, Chile and Argentina.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Aymara lordships (page read); Wikipedia: Aymara people (search excerpt)

neighbours.value: Cuzco and the Inca to the north; non-Aymara peoples such as the Chuy and Yampara lay beside the Charcas group in the south.
neighbours.source: Penn DIA, map summary of the Qullasuyu / Charcas Altiplano (BOL0028Y)

ideasReligions.value: The kingdoms developed after Tiwanaku fell, and Aymara migration helped break up Wari control.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Aymara lordships (page read); Wikipedia: Pre-Columbian Bolivia (mirror excerpts)

colonisation.value: The Spanish conquest later began to dismember the territory.

riseSignals.value: The kingdoms grew after the fall of Tiwanaku and the weakening of Wari; Wikipedia gives c. 1151 as the start.

peakPeriod.value: Between about 1100 and 1460 the Aymara built kingdoms around Lake Titicaca, of which the Lupaca, Colla and Cana were the largest.

declineSignals.value: Inca expansion from about 1440 and revolts by the lake kingdoms against Inca demands for land and labour.

outcome.value: Absorbed into the Inca state; Wikipedia's infobox gives 1477 as the end, another account puts the conquest under Huayna Capac, and the kingdoms remained relatively autonomous inside the empire.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Aymara lordships (page read); Wikipedia: Aymara people (search excerpt); Wikipedia: Prehistory of Bolivia (excerpt)

sources.value: Read: one full page (Wikipedia, Aymara lordships) and search excerpts of Encyclopedia.com (Aymara), Wikipedia mirrors on Pre-Columbian Bolivia and Aymara people, and a Penn DIA map summary; 17 Nov 2026. Several Wikipedia statements are uncited there, and the page says nothing on diet or fortifications.

overallCertainty.value: No written record before the Inca; Spanish chroniclers and archaeology carry the story, and dates for the lordships and the Inca conquest differ by source (1151 to 1477, or under Huayna Capac after 1493).
